title: Determination of the properties of a superconducting single crystal FeSe using an EPR spectroscopy
authors: S. I. Bondarenko, A. A. Prokhorov, N. N. Galtsov, V. P. Timofeev, V. P. Koverya, A. V. Krevsun
abstract: Using an EPR spectrometer, the properties of single-crystal FeSe were studied in a magnetic field up to 6000 Oe at temperatures from 3.5 K to 8 K in the superconducting state and at temperatures above 8K and up to 25K in the normal state. It was shown that by measuring non-resonant spectrometer signals in zero and weak magnetic fields up to 30 Oe, it is possible to determine critical temperature Tc, the superconducting transition width, and the value of the first critical magnetic field Hc1 in FeSe single-crystal. Resonant EPR signals are observed in fields at 1400 Oe and 3400 Oe, which corresponds to the paramagnetism of doubly ionized iron atoms (Fe2+) in the FeSe crystal. Non-resonant EPR signals in a magnetic field up to 6000 Oe at temperatures from 3.5K to 8K are a nonlinear function of the field, and correspond to the superconducting mixed state of the FeSe, but at temperatures above 8K (up to 25K) they are field independent.
summary: This work uses Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy on FeSe single crystals to characterize their superconducting properties. By analyzing non-resonant EPR signals under varying magnetic fields and temperatures, the authors determined critical parameters such as $T_c$ and $H_{c1}$. The results confirm the mixed state behavior expected for a Type-II superconductor while also identifying electronic signatures related to iron ion oxidation states.
main_problem: To study the superconducting and normal state properties of a single crystal of FeSe using Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy.
main_result: The EPR measurements successfully determined key superconducting parameters like $T_c$, the transition width, and the first critical magnetic field ($H_{c1}$), while also characterizing the electronic states via resonant signals corresponding to $	ext{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.
method: EPR spectroscopy was employed across varying temperatures and applied magnetic fields. Non-resonant signals were analyzed for superconducting signatures (e.g., $180^\circ$ phase jumps), while resonant signals identified specific paramagnetic ion states.
model_or_system: The physical system is a single crystal of FeSe, studied as a Type-II superconductor. Measurements compare the field dependence of non-resonant EPR signals in the mixed state to theoretical models derived from the temperature derivative of resistivity ($dR^*/dT$).
key_observables: Non-resonant EPR signal (field/temperature dependent), resonant EPR signals at 1400 Oe and 3400 Oe, $T_c$, superconducting transition width, and $H_{c1}$.
important_parameters: Magnetic field up to 6000 Oe; Temperature range from 3.5 K to 25 K; Critical fields ($H_{c1}$) and onset temperature ($T_{c	ext{onset}} \approx 8.8 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The non-resonant EPR signal is proportional to the field derivative of the radiation power, and comparisons between electrical (FPM) and microwave (EPR) measurements are made despite methodological differences.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $T_{c	ext{onset}}$ from magnetization ($T_c=8.8 	ext{ K}$), the nonlinear field dependence of the EPR signal in the mixed state, the characteristic $180^\circ$ phase jump identifying $H_{c1}$, and comparisons between temperature-dependent EPR signals and resistivity derivatives.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents measurements across different states (normal vs. superconducting) using EPR. It first establishes $T_c$ via magnetization, then uses low-field non-resonant signals to map the mixed state behavior ($H_{c1}$ identification), and finally compares the temperature dependence of these signals against established electrical transport models.
why_interesting: The use of high-frequency EPR spectroscopy to probe superconducting vortex dynamics and critical fields provides an alternative, highly sensitive diagnostic tool compared to standard DC magnetometry or resistivity measurements in condensed matter physics.
